content.title: About
content.content: Bread made from wheat or cracked wheat is one of the most widely consumed foods worldwide. Wheat is a cereal grain rich in carbohydrates, protein, B‑vitamins and minerals. Cracked wheat (often called bulgur) is used in baking, porridges and as an addition to dough, giving a denser texture and a characteristic nutty flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Wheat was domesticated more than 10,000 years ago in the Fertile Crescent.
There are over 25,000 wheat varieties, differing in gluten content and flavor profiles.
Cracked wheat is commonly referred to as bulgur, although bulgur is usually pre‑cooked before drying.
Whole‑grain wheat bread retains most of the bran and germ, making it more nutritious than white bread.
In many cultures (e.g., Mediterranean) wheat bread is a symbol of hospitality and prosperity.

items.title: Rich in complex carbohydrates
items.content: Wheat provides a slow release of energy, helping to maintain stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: About 13 g of protein per 100 g of wheat makes it a valuable addition to vegetarian diets.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Thiamine, niacin and folate support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain bread promotes digestive health and contributes to satiety.

items.title: Minerals: iron, magnesium, zinc
items.content: These trace elements are involved in hemoglobin formation, muscle function and immune response.

items.title: Gluten intolerance
items.content: People with celiac disease or non‑celiac gluten sensitivity may experience intestinal inflammation and other symptoms after consuming wheat.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Refined white wheat bread can cause rapid spikes in blood sugar, which is undesirable for diabetics.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: Some wheat crops may contain pesticide residues; choosing organic or certified sources can reduce this risk.

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: Rare but possible, it can manifest as skin rashes, swelling or gastrointestinal discomfort.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Whole‑grain wheat bread can be enjoyed on its own, as toast, in sandwiches or served alongside soups. Cracked wheat is used in salads, as a base for couscous, in hot porridges, or added to dough to improve texture and flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store bread in a cool, dry place in a paper bag or bread box to keep the crust crisp. Keep cracked wheat in an airtight container in the refrigerator or a dark, cool pantry to preserve its aroma and prevent mold.

breakfast-bar-cereal-crust-with-fruit-fi.title: Breakfast Bar, Cereal Crust with Fruit Filling, Low‑Fat

content.title: About
content.content: The breakfast bar features a crunchy cereal crust filled with a fruit puree. It is low‑fat (about 2 g per 100 g) and designed for a quick morning meal or snack. The bar contains whole grains, dried fruit, and a modest amount of sweetener.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The bar combines a crisp grain base with a naturally sweet fruit filling, without artificial flavors.
Its low‑fat formula reduces calories while preserving taste.
Whole grains such as oats and wheat are used, retaining most of the dietary fiber.
The fruit filling is typically made from berries and apples, boosting vitamin C content.
Products are often packaged in single‑serve portions, convenient for travel and sport.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Whole grains and dried fruit provide dietary fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: Only about 2 g of fat per 100 g makes it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Oats and wheat supply thiamine, riboflavin, and niacin, which aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Fruit filling, especially from berries, is rich in polyphenols that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports blood‑sugar stability
items.content: The low glycemic index of whole grains together with fruit filling helps maintain steady glucose levels after eating.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The bar contains wheat, so it is not suitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Although marketed as low‑fat, the fruit filling may contain added sugars; those monitoring sugar intake should consider this.

items.title: Food additives
items.content: Some versions may include preservatives or stabilizers that could trigger reactions in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Eat the bar straight from the package as a quick breakfast or snack. It can also be chopped and added to yogurt, kefir, or a smoothie for extra volume and nutrition.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the bar in a dry, cool place away from direct sunlight. After opening, consume within 7‑10 days, or keep refrigerated for longer shelf life.

content.title: About
content.content: Cereal is a ready‑to‑eat breakfast made from whole or processed grains (wheat, oats, rice, corn, etc.) that are toasted, often sweetened, and formed into flakes. The product has a light, crunchy texture and a neutral flavor, making it a popular quick‑morning option.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first ready‑made cereal was created in the late 19th century by John Harvey Kellogg in the United States.
There are more than 30 varieties, including whole‑grain, gluten‑free, and vitamin‑fortified options.
Cereal is frequently used as a base for granola bars, muesli, and dessert recipes.
In many countries it is served with milk, yogurt, fruit, or nuts.
Fortified cereals may contain added B‑vitamins, iron, and calcium.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Cereal provides slowly digestible energy, helping to maintain satiety for several hours.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain versions contain fiber that supports healthy digestion and gut microbiota.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B1, B2, B6 and folate aid carbohydrate metabolism and support the nervous system.

items.title: Fortified with minerals
items.content: Many cereals are enriched with iron, calcium and magnesium to help address common deficiencies.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Unlike many processed breakfasts, plain cereal typically contains little fat unless nuts or oils are added.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Sweetened cereals can contain up to 30 % sugar, increasing the risk of cavities and weight gain.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Most wheat, barley or rye cereals contain gluten and are unsuitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Some varieties include nuts, soy protein or dairy additives that may trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Additive concerns
items.content: Artificial flavors and preservatives can cause sensitivity in certain individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cereal is typically poured over milk, kefir, or a plant‑based drink and left for 1–2 minutes. It can be topped with fresh berries, banana slices, nuts, honey, or dried fruit to boost nutritional value.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cereal in a sealed package in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, transfer to an airtight container to prevent moisture absorption and loss of crunch.

chicken-fillet-sandwich-grilled-on-white.title: Chicken Fillet Sandwich, Grilled, on White Bun

content.title: About
content.content: The grilled chicken fillet sandwich is served on a soft white bun. It features tender chicken fillet lightly charred on the grill, fresh vegetables, and a choice of sauce. A quick and satisfying option for lunch or a snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Grilling chicken fillet retains more protein compared to deep‑frying.
White buns are popular in fast food for their neutral flavor that highlights the filling.
Chicken sandwiches are a common choice in moderate‑fat diets.
Chicken meat is rich in B‑vitamins, especially niacin (B3).
Some restaurants add spices like paprika and garlic to boost flavor.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken fillet provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Grilling reduces added fat compared with frying, making it a leaner option.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B6 and B12 support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: Chicken supplies phosphorus, selenium, and zinc, important for bones and immunity.

items.title: Moderate calories
items.content: The sandwich provides energy without excessive calories when a low‑fat sauce is chosen.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Sauces and buns can be high in salt; individuals with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Cross‑contamination risk
items.content: When grilling, avoid contact with raw meat to prevent foodborne illness.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sandwich is ready to eat straight from the grill. It can be halved, topped with fresh lettuce, tomato or cucumber, and paired with a sauce such as mayo, mustard, or yogurt.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared sandwich in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours in an airtight container. For longer storage, keep ingredients separate and assemble the sandwich before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Honey mustard dressing is a blend of honey, Dijon mustard, vinegar and vegetable oil. It has a sweet‑tangy flavor that pairs well with salads, chicken, fish and vegetable dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The honey‑mustard combination has been used in cooking since ancient Rome.
There are many variations, including additions of soy sauce, garlic or fresh herbs.
Honey mustard is often served in restaurants as a salad dressing and as a sauce for grilled meats.
Mustard contains sinigrin, which gives a mild heat without harsh spiciness.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Honey provides flavonoids and mustard adds sinigrin, both acting as antioxidants.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Mustard seeds stimulate bile production, aiding digestive processes.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: The dressing contains small amounts of vitamins B1, B2 and B6, important for metabolism.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: Vegetable oil supplies monounsaturated fatty acids that are heart‑friendly.

items.title: Allergy to honey or mustard
items.content: Individuals allergic to honey or mustard may experience reactions up to anaphylaxis.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Honey adds sweetness, so people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some commercial versions contain added salt; those with hypertension should choose low‑sodium options.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Use the dressing to drizzle salads, as a marinade for chicken, fish or tofu, dip for vegetable sticks, fries, or as a dip for appetizers.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the dressing in a sealed jar in the refrigerator. Once opened it stays fresh for 1–2 weeks. Discard if the smell changes or mold appears.

content.title: About
content.content: Lo mein is a Chinese dish consisting of stir‑fried wheat noodles, often combined with vegetables, soy sauce, and various add‑ins. The chicken version uses boiled chicken breast sliced into strips, giving the dish a tender flavor and boosting its protein content.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lo mein originates from Jiangsu province, where thin wheat noodles have been traditionally used.
In Japan a similar dish is ramen, though Japanese noodles are usually chewier.
Chicken for lo mein is often marinated in soy sauce, ginger, and garlic to enhance aroma.
The dish is a staple of street stalls and fast‑casual restaurants worldwide.
Traditionally lo mein is cooked over high heat, quickly stir‑frying ingredients to keep the noodles crisp.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Chicken breast provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains complex carbohydrates
items.content: Wheat noodles supply slowly digestible carbs that sustain energy levels.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Ingredients such as soy sauce and vegetables add B1, B2, and B6 vitamins important for metabolism.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: When prepared with moderate oil, the dish remains relatively low‑calorie and suitable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Antioxidants from vegetables
items.content: Carrots, bell peppers, and green onions provide carotenoids and vitamin C, supporting immune health.

items.title: Soy sauce allergy
items.content: Soy sauce can trigger allergic reactions in individuals with soy sensitivity.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Traditional soy sauce is salty; people with hypertension should limit its use.

items.title: Monosodium glutamate (MSG)
items.content: Some sauces contain added MSG, which may cause sensitivity in certain individuals.

items.title: Cooking temperature control
items.content: Over‑cooking the noodles can produce acrylamide, a potentially harmful compound.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve chicken lo mein hot, often garnished with sliced green onions, sesame seeds, or fresh cilantro. Adjust flavor with extra soy sauce, chili, or a squeeze of lime as desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2–3 days. Reheat in a skillet or microwave, adding a little oil to restore the noodles’ crispness.

content.title: About
content.content: Margarine is a vegetable fat obtained by hydrogenating plant oils. It is used as a butter substitute in cooking and baking. Margarine has a soft texture, a mild buttery flavor, and typically lower saturated fat content than traditional butter.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first commercial margarine was created in 1869 by French chemist Hippolyte Mège-Mouriès.
In Russia margarine is often labeled as "vegetable oil" in the food industry.
Margarine can be fortified with vitamins A and D to compensate for their absence in plant oils.
Hydrogenation gives margarine a solid structure at room temperature, which is convenient for baking.
Some margarines are enriched with omega‑3 fatty acids.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with butter, margarine usually contains less saturated fat, which may help lower cholesterol levels.

items.title: Source of vitamin E
items.content: Vitamin E present in plant oils acts as an antioxidant, protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Fortified with vitamins A and D
items.content: Certain brands are additionally enriched with vitamins A and D, supporting vision and bone health.

items.title: Convenient to use
items.content: Margarine softens easily, remains stable during storage, and is suitable for a wide range of culinary tasks.

items.title: Trans fats
items.content: Some margarines produced by partial hydrogenation may contain trans fats, which increase the risk of cardiovascular disease.

items.title: Allergy to plant oils
items.content: Individuals may be allergic to soy or sunflower oils commonly used in margarine.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: As a fat, margarine is energy‑dense; excessive consumption can contribute to weight gain.

items.title: Additives and preservatives
items.content: Certain brands contain artificial flavors, emulsifiers, and preservatives that may be undesirable for sensitive people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Margarine is used as a butter substitute on sandwiches, for frying, and in baking cakes, cookies, and croissants. It can be spread on bread, added to sauces and creams. For baking, choose a margarine with higher water content for a lighter crumb.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store margarine in the refrigerator in its original packaging or an airtight container. At room temperature it may soften but remains usable for up to 2 weeks. Discard if it develops off‑odors, discoloration, or mold.

content.title: About
content.content: The Sandwich Wrap NFS (1654) is a soft wheat tortilla designed for quick preparation of sandwiches and wraps. It has a mild flavor, light texture, and is convenient for both home and professional kitchens.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dough contains a small amount of yeast, giving the wrap a subtle airy lift.
The original recipe uses milk, making the product softer than typical flatbreads.
NFS wraps are popular in fast‑food and cafeteria settings because they only need a quick heat‑up.
The wrap works well with both cold and hot fillings.
Packaging usually contains 10–12 pieces, ideal for portion planning.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: The wrap provides a fast‑acting source of energy through easily digestible carbs.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many baked goods, the sandwich wrap contains minimal fat.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Whole wheat flour contributes vitamins B1, B2 and niacin.

items.title: Pairs well with protein
items.content: The wrap complements meat, fish, or legumes, creating a balanced meal.

items.title: Portion control friendly
items.content: Standardized size helps accurately calculate caloric intake.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Contains wheat, making it unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some versions add salt, which may be a concern for those with hypertension.

items.title: Short shelf life after opening
items.content: Once opened, the wraps lose moisture quickly and can become stiff.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use the wrap as a base for cold sandwiches, hot burgers, or rolled fillings with chicken, vegetables, or seafood. For hot applications, warm the wrap in an oven or skillet until lightly golden.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the wraps in a cool, dry place, in the original packaging or an airtight container. After opening, consume within 3–5 days. They can be frozen for up to 2 months if needed.
